titre: Sutherland, 1949: White-Collar Crime, Without the Names
accroche: In 1949, Sutherland publishes a study of 70 large American corporations. The names are gone; they will not return until 1983.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Table 3 of the 1949 book, the seventy large American corporations studied bear no names: they are numbered from 1 to 70. The court and commission decisions targeting them are counted, but there is no way to say who is concerned. This is the state in which *White Collar Crime*, by Edwin H. Sutherland, circulated for more than thirty years.

## The Mechanism

Sutherland had introduced the expression “white-collar crime” in 1939, in Philadelphia, at a joint meeting of the American Sociological Society, of which he was president, and the American Economic Association. He used it to designate offenses committed by respected people in the course of their occupation: fraud, false advertising, bribes, violations of antitrust legislation. The text appeared in 1940 in the *American Sociological Review*, under the title “White-Collar Criminality.”

A decade of work follows. Since 1928, Sutherland had students collect reports on corporate offenses. The book appears in 1949 from Dryden Press. But, according to the sociologist Gilbert Geis, the publishers feared libel suits: Sutherland calls criminal corporations whose offenses had not been handled by a criminal court. Chapters are cut, including, according to Joseph Belth's account, the one with the three case studies. According to Belth, the administration of Indiana University, which feared alienating major donors, also pressured Sutherland, who ended up accepting the cuts. Again according to Belth, who consulted the original manuscript at the Lilly Library of Indiana University, the names are replaced by numbers and by letters, and the references to the decisions, which would have made it possible to identify the corporations, are removed. In his preface, Sutherland justifies this choice by the custom of withholding offenders' identities in scientific writing, and by the book's aim, the theory of criminal behavior. He admits that this loses the effect of reality of the documented cases, while judging that the book's logic does not suffer from it. The 1961 edition remains cut in the same way.

## What It Shifts

The uncut text is not published until 1983, more than thirty years later: *White Collar Crime: The Uncut Version*, from Yale University Press, with an introduction by Gilbert Geis and Colin Goff. Sutherland had died in 1950.

The publishers' fear touches the heart of the debate. Sutherland maintains that these offenses are crimes even when the legal system handles them in civil or administrative proceedings: just as a tuberculosis patient remains a tuberculosis patient whatever the treatment, the perpetrator of such an offense remains a criminal, whether it is discovered or not. Paul Tappan reproaches him in 1947 for providing no precise criterion and for wielding a term that may be nothing but propaganda.

The theoretical stakes are just as clear. According to Geis, white-collar crime serves as a polemical trump card for Sutherland against the explanations of crime prevailing in his day, such as mental deficiency, poverty, immigration, broken homes, or the Oedipus complex: if elite offenders, perpetrators of antitrust violations for example, do not show the personal or social characteristics linked to crime, these characteristics cannot be held to be the explanation of all crime.

The debate turned on this question: who decides that an act is a crime, the court or the sociologist?

repere.texte: In 1983, Yale University Press publishes White Collar Crime: The Uncut Version, which restores the names and identifications removed from the 1949 study of seventy large American corporations.
repere.source: Sutherland, White Collar Crime: The Uncut Version, Yale University Press, 1983 (Internet Archive record)

carte.punch: The 1949 book on 70 large corporations appears without their names: lawsuits were feared.
carte.idee: Sutherland introduces “white-collar crime” in 1939. His 1949 book on 70 large American corporations appears without their names, his publishers fearing libel suits; the uncut text does not come out until 1983, from Yale University Press.

The detail of what was removed in 1949.

quiz.question: Why were the names of the corporations studied by Sutherland removed from the 1949 edition?
choix: Because Sutherland had not been able to verify the identity of these corporations with the courts and preferred not to name them
Because the publishers feared libel suits: Sutherland called criminal corporations that had not been tried in criminal court
Because the targeted corporations had obtained a court ban on publishing the first version of the book
Because Sutherland had died before publication and his heirs had removed the names
quiz.explication: According to Geis, the publishers notably feared libel suits, Sutherland calling criminal corporations whose offenses had not been handled in criminal court; Cressey also writes this in 1961. Sutherland accepted the cuts and justified them in his preface. The removal was due neither to a failure of verification, nor to a court ban, nor to his death (he died in 1950, after the 1949 publication), and the uncut text did not appear until 1983.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does Sutherland first introduce the expression “white-collar crime”?
choix: In 1939, in Philadelphia, at a joint meeting of two learned associations
In 1949, in the preface of his book White Collar Crime
In 1928, at the launch of his program of collecting corporate offenses
In 1947, in direct response to Paul Tappan's criticism
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sutherland introduces the expression in 1939 in Philadelphia, at a joint meeting of the American Sociological Society, of which he was president, and the American Economic Association; the text appeared in 1940 in the American Sociological Review.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Sutherland, in what way does a business executive who committed a white-collar offense remain a criminal, even without a criminal conviction?
choix: Because the law always catches up with him sooner or later
Because the press has already judged him publicly before any trial
Just as a tuberculosis patient remains a tuberculosis patient whatever the treatment, a criminal remains one too
Because the corporations concerned ended up acknowledging the facts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sutherland maintains that these offenses are crimes even when handled in civil or administrative proceedings: just as a tuberculosis patient remains a tuberculosis patient whatever the treatment, the perpetrator of such an offense remains a criminal, whether it is discovered or not.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Gilbert Geis, what does the argument of white-collar crime serve for in Sutherland's theory?
choix: To prove that only large corporations commit crimes
To demonstrate that white-collar crime is less serious than street crime
To justify a reform of corporate criminal law proposed by Sutherland himself
As a polemical trump card against the explanations of crime prevailing in his day, such as poverty or broken homes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Geis, if elite offenders, such as perpetrators of antitrust violations, do not show the personal or social traits linked to crime (poverty, broken homes, etc.), these traits cannot explain all crime.
